::: notes
Yes. A perfect square is m^2 for a positive integer m, and
m^2 = T_{m-1} + T_m, so the witness is k = m.

Both definitions are for positive integers, so 0 never comes up, and T_0 = 0
is defined, so 1 = T_0 + T_1 is a glow number.

The theorem and its converse together: the glow numbers are exactly the
perfect squares. Proving the converse means naming a k for a given m -- an
existential, proved by giving the witness.
:::

## Sudoku Warm Up {.activity}

In a 4x4 Sudoku, each row, each column and each 2x2 box contains each of 1, 2, 3
and 4 exactly once.

Solve the Sudoku on the worksheet.

Speculate on an interesting feature of the corners.

Do all 4x4 Sudoku puzzles have this feature?

{{< countdown minutes=5 >}}

::: notes
The puzzle has exactly one solution:
  2 3 4 1
  1 4 2 3
  4 1 3 2
  3 2 1 4
Its four corners (2, 1, 3, 4) are all different.

Do all 4x4 sudokus have that? NO -- only 168 of the 288. Counterexample:
  1 2 3 4 / 3 4 1 2 / 2 1 4 3 / 4 3 2 1   -- corners 1, 4, 4, 1.

"THIS feature" (the a b c d corners against the * centre) is the next slide, Corners and
Centre, with the proof in its notes.

A speculation checked on one example is not a theorem -- that is the point to
land before the proofs.
:::

## Corners and Centre

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 326 326" width="400" height="400" role="img" aria-label="4 by 4 sudoku grid with corners a, b, c, d and the four centre cells starred">
<g transform="translate(3,3)">

<line x1="0" y1="240" x2="320" y2="240" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1.5"/>

<text x="40.0" y="52.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#999">a</text>
<text x="280.0" y="52.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#999">b</text>
<text x="40.0" y="292.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#999">c</text>
<text x="280.0" y="292.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#999">d</text>
<text x="120.0" y="132.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#999">&#42;</text>
<text x="200.0" y="132.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#999">&#42;</text>
<text x="120.0" y="212.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#999">&#42;</text>

</g>
</svg>
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Do all 4x4 Sudoku puzzles have THIS feature?
:::
::::

::: notes
YES, in all 288: the four corners (a, b, c, d) hold exactly the same four
numbers as the four centre cells (*). Not cell by cell -- the four together.

The proof never looks at a single cell. Rows and columns are the only
collections whose contents we know (each is exactly 1, 2, 3, 4), so count with
those, and treat each set of cells as a bag of numbers, duplicates kept.

  The four rows: every cell once.
    = four copies of {1,2,3,4} = corners + border + centre
  Rows 1 and 4, plus columns 1 and 4: the four edges. The centre is not in
  them, and each corner is in one of those rows AND one of those columns, so
  the corners are counted twice.
    = four copies of {1,2,3,4} = corners + corners + border
  Same bag, so corners + border + centre = corners + corners + border.
  Take one copy of the corners and the border off both sides:
    centre = corners.

(border = the 8 edge cells that are not corners.)

Check on the worksheet's solution 2341 / 1423 / 4132 / 3214: corners 2, 1, 3, 4;
centre 4, 2, 1, 3. Same four numbers.

Not cell by cell: a centre cell is never equal to the corner in its own box, but
it can equal any of the other three. In 1234 / 3412 / 2143 / 4321, r2c2 = 4
matches r1c4 and r4c1, not the far corner r4c4 = 1.

It never uses the boxes: true for all 576 grids whose rows and columns each
hold 1-4. (A 9x9 version of the same argument is known as the Phistomefel ring.)
:::

## $\to$ Sudoku: Direct

:::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
Prove that for any solution to this mini sudoku, if the solution has a 2 in the
top-left square (r1c1), then it has a 2 in the bottom-right square (r4c4).
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/images/sudokupf1.png)
:::
::::

::: notes
Scrutinize the form of the statement: for any solution, if P then Q.

Assume r1c1 = 2. Row 1 then holds 1, 2 and 3, so r1c4 = 4. Column 4 holds 4,
1 and 3, so r4c4 = 2. Done -- two steps.

Checked against all 4x4 sudokus: the puzzle has 6 solutions, and in the 3
where r1c1 = 2, r4c4 = 2.
:::

## $\leftrightsquigarrow$ Sudoku: Contrapositive

::::: columns

::: {.column width="35%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 204 204" width="230" height="230" role="img" aria-label="4 by 4 sudoku grid; the top-left 2 by 2 box has cells A, B, C, D">
<g transform="translate(2,2)">
<rect x="0" y="0" width="100" height="100" fill="#e8eef5"/>
<line x1="50" y1="0" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1"/>
<line x1="0" y1="50" x2="200" y2="50" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1"/>
<line x1="100" y1="0" x2="100" y2="200" stroke="#333" stroke-width="4"/>
<line x1="0" y1="100" x2="200" y2="100" stroke="#333" stroke-width="4"/>
<line x1="150" y1="0" x2="150" y2="200" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1"/>
<line x1="0" y1="150" x2="200" y2="150" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1"/>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="200" height="200" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="4"/>
<text x="25.0" y="34.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#333">A</text>
<text x="75.0" y="34.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#333">B</text>
<text x="25.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#333">C</text>
<text x="75.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26" font-family="sans-serif" fill="#333">D</text>
</g>
</svg>
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
Theorem: For any valid Sudoku solution, if A and B and C are not 4, then D is 4.
:::
:::::

Contrapositive:

::: notes
If D is not 4, then A or B or C is 4.

The negation of "A and B and C are not 4" is "A or B or C is 4" -- De Morgan,
worth pointing at.

Proof: the box contains a 4 somewhere. It is not D, so it is A, B or C. The
contrapositive is the easy direction here: it is just "the 4 has to be
somewhere".
:::

## ↯ Sudoku: Contradiction

:::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
Prove that any solution to this mini sudoku has a 3 in the top-right corner
(r1c4).
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/images/04_tue_argument21.jpg){width="80%"}
:::
::::

::: notes
Scrutinize the form: "any solution has a 3 at r1c4".

Suppose r1c4 is not 3. Row 1 needs a 3. Not c1 (column 1 has the 3 at r3c1),
not c2 (that is the 2), not c4 (assumed). So r1c3 = 3.

The bottom-right box needs a 3. Not in row 3 (row 3 has its 3 at r3c1), and
r4c4 is 1, so r4c3 = 3. Now column 3 has two 3s -- r1c3 and r4c3.
Contradiction.

Checked: the puzzle has 3 solutions and r1c4 = 3 in all of them; with r1c3 = 3
added there are none.
:::

## Today’s goals

- Understand role of components of an inductive proof.
- Write short inductive proofs.


## Warm Up {.activity}

A *Tower* is built by stacking 5m red panels, and 7m blue panels.

What tower heights are possible? Talk it through with the people around you:
which heights can you build, and which can't you?

{{< countdown minutes=10 >}}

::: notes
Give this time -- it took a while last year. Let them find the last height
that cannot be built (23) themselves.

End up with a clear claim: For all n > 23, we can build a tower of
height n using only 5m red and 7m blue panels.

Say "claim holds for smaller values"
:::

## Warm Up Continued {.smaller}

Claim: for all integers $n > 23$, we can build a tower of height
$n$ using only 5m red and 7m blue panels.

::: {.fillable}
| Height | Red | Blue |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 24 | | |
| 25 | | |
| 26 | | |
| 27 | | |
| 28 | | |
: {tbl-colwidths="[30,35,35]"}
:::

Every height $n \geq 29$: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
24 = 2 red + 2 blue. 25 = 5 red. 26 = 1 red + 3 blue. 27 = 4 red + 1 blue.
28 = 4 blue.

Every n >= 29: n - 5 is at least 24, so a tower of height n - 5 can be built.
Add one red panel.

Why FIVE base cases: each height comes from the height 5 below it, so the
first five have to be checked by hand. Three is not enough -- 28 would need
23, which cannot be built. (27 would need 22, which can be built, but the claim
says nothing about 22.) Worth asking before filling in the table.

Point out the universal quantifier, and the least value. This is proof by
cases plus one new move: assume it for a smaller value (n - 5). That is
induction, before it has a name.

Aside, only if it comes up: 23 = 5*7 - 5 - 7.
:::

## Inductive Proof Skeleton Card


<div class="card">

Proof by Induction of $\forall n, P(n)$

1. First line: "Consider an arbitrary n." 
2. Second line (IH): "Assume $\forall j < n, P(j)$."
3. Determine exhaustive cases for $n$, including one or more base cases and usually one inductive case.
4. Prove each case, base and inductive, independently. Base case is typically direct, and inductive case will require use of IH.

</div>

## Proof by Induction {.smaller}

Claim: For any integer $n > 0$, $\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n} k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$.

\

Proof: Consider an arbitrary integer $n > 0$. 

\

IH: Assume inductively that for any $j<n$, $\sum\limits_{k=1}^{j} k^2 = \frac{j(j+1)(2j+1)}{6}$.

\

Either $n=1$, or $n>1$.

Case 1 $(n=1)$:

\

Case 2 $(n>1)$:

Claim: For any $n>0$, $\sum\limits_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{(2k-1)(2k+1)} = \frac{n}{2n+1}$.

If this runs over, it opens Wednesday: the sum telescopes, which is L12's
